# Transverse modes and line broadening {#sec-broadening} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/broadening.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slide 75 (transverse laser modes) and slides 76–83 (homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening, Lorentzian and Gaussian line shapes, Doppler broadening, spectral hole burning, summary table).* ## Key relations **Transverse modes** (slide 75). Real mirrors are curved and finite, so the field that reproduces itself after a round trip is not a plane wave but a Gaussian beam (Ch. 1) multiplied by Hermite polynomials. The TEM$_{mn}$ mode has $m$ nodes along $x$ and $n$ along $y$: $$ E_{mn}(x,y)\propto H_m\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2x}{w}\right)H_n\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2y}{w}\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{w^2}\right). $$ TEM$_{00}$ is the Gaussian beam with the smallest divergence; most lasers are designed to emit only this mode. **Line broadening** (slides 76–83). An emitting transition is never infinitely sharp. * **Homogeneous** broadening affects all atoms in the same way: lifetime (natural) broadening, collisions in a gas, phonon collisions in a crystal. A field that decays as $E_0e^{-t/2\tau_2}\cos\omega_0t$ has a **Lorentzian** spectrum (slides 77–78), $$g_L(\nu)=\frac{\gamma/\pi}{(\nu-\nu_0)^2+\gamma^2},\qquad \Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\gamma=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau_2}.$$ * **Inhomogeneous** broadening gives different atoms different centre frequencies: Doppler shifts in a gas, random local fields in a glass. The line is the envelope of many narrow lines, usually a **Gaussian** (slides 79–80), $$g_G(\nu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\nu-\nu_0)^2}{\Gamma^2}\right],\qquad \Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\Gamma\sqrt{\ln2}.$$ When both act, the line is their convolution, the **Voigt** profile. ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"} ## Lifetime broadening on slide 78 Slide 78 writes "$1/\gamma=\tau_2$" with $\Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\gamma$. For the field $E_0e^{-t/2\tau_2}\cos\omega_0t$ written on the same slide, the Fourier transform gives a Lorentzian with $\Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=1/(2\pi\tau_2)$, that is $\gamma=1/(4\pi\tau_2)$. The statement $1/\gamma=\tau_2$ holds for the **angular** half width when the field (not the intensity) decays with $\tau_2$. The factor $4\pi$ matters: a 100 ns Ne level has a natural width of 1.6 MHz, not 20 MHz. Slide 80 also writes the normalisation as $\int g_L\,d\nu=1$ under the Gaussian; it should read $g_G$. ::: ## Transverse modes (slide 75) ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof tm = Inputs.form({ m: Inputs.range([0, 6], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "m (nodes along x)"}), n: Inputs.range([0, 6], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "n (nodes along y)"}), donut: Inputs.toggle({label: "add the rotated mode with a 90° phase (TEM₀₁* 'donut')", value: false}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false tmOut = { const H = (k, x) => { let h0 = 1, h1 = 2*x; if (k === 0) return h0; for (let i = 1; i < k; i++) { const h2 = 2*x*h1 - 2*i*h0; h0 = h1; h1 = h2; } return h1; }; const N = 121, ext = 3.2, v = new Float64Array(N*N); for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { const x = -ext + 2*ext*i/(N - 1), y = -ext + 2*ext*j/(N - 1), g = Math.exp(-(x*x + y*y)); const a = H(tm.m, Math.SQRT2*x)*H(tm.n, Math.SQRT2*y)*g, b = H(tm.n, Math.SQRT2*x)*H(tm.m, Math.SQRT2*y)*g; v[j*N + i] = tm.donut ? a*a + b*b : a*a; } const mx = d3.max(v); for (let k = 0; k < v.length; k++) v[k] /= mx; return {v, N, ext}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 420), height: Math.min(width, 420), aspectRatio: 1, x: {label: "x/w", domain: [-tmOut.ext, tmOut.ext]}, y: {label: "y/w", domain: [-tmOut.ext, tmOut.ext]}, color: {scheme: "magma"}, marks: [Plot.raster(tmOut.v, {width: tmOut.N, height: tmOut.N, x1: -tmOut.ext, x2: tmOut.ext, y1: -tmOut.ext, y2: tmOut.ext, interpolate: "nearest"})] }) ``` Each transverse mode $(m,n)$ has its own set of longitudinal resonances, shifted from those of TEM$_{00}$ by the Gouy phase. A laser that oscillates on several transverse modes therefore emits extra frequencies and a larger, irregular beam. The frequencies and the mode size follow from the mirror curvatures: see [Going further: optical resonators](resonators.qmd). An aperture inside the cavity (or, in a laser diode, a narrow stripe, @sec-ld-structures) adds loss to the wider high-order modes and keeps only TEM$_{00}$. ## Line shapes (slides 77–81) ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof ls = Inputs.form({ fL: Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Lorentzian (homogeneous) FWHM"}), fG: Inputs.range([0, 5], {value: 1.5, step: 0.05, label: "Gaussian (inhomogeneous) FWHM"}), log: Inputs.toggle({label: "log scale (look at the wings)", value: false}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false lsOut = { const N = 2001, span = 12, dx = 2*span/(N - 1), xs = d3.range(N).map(i => -span + i*dx); const gam = Math.max(ls.fL, 1e-3)/2, G = Math.max(ls.fG, 1e-3)/(2*Math.sqrt(Math.LN2)); const L = xs.map(x => (gam/Math.PI)/(x*x + gam*gam)), Ga = xs.map(x => Math.exp(-(x*x)/(G*G))/(Math.sqrt(Math.PI)*G)); const V = xs.map((x, i) => { let s = 0; for (let k = 0; k < N; k += 2) s += Ga[k]*(gam/Math.PI)/((x - xs[k])**2 + gam*gam); return s*2*dx; }); const fwhm = arr => { const m = d3.max(arr), idx = arr.map((v, i) => v >= m/2 ? i : -1).filter(i => i >= 0); return (idx[idx.length - 1] - idx[0])*dx; }; const data = xs.flatMap((x, i) => [{x, y: L[i], who: "Lorentzian"}, {x, y: Ga[i], who: "Gaussian"}, {x, y: V[i], who: "Voigt (convolution)"}]); return {data, fV: fwhm(V), approx: 0.5346*ls.fL + Math.sqrt(0.2166*ls.fL**2 + ls.fG**2)}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 300, x: {label: "ν − ν₀ (same units as the FWHMs)", domain: [-8, 8]}, y: {label: "g(ν) (normalised, area = 1)", type: ls.log ? "log" : "linear", grid: true, domain: ls.log ? [1e-4, 2] : undefined}, color: {legend: true, range: ["#eb6834", "#2a78d6", "#1baf7a"]}, marks: [Plot.line(lsOut.data.filter(d => !ls.log || d.y > 1e-5), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
Voigt FWHM = ${lsOut.fV.toFixed(3)} (Olivero approximation 0.5346 fL + √(0.2166 fL² + fG²) = ${lsOut.approx.toFixed(3)})
` ``` With the same FWHM, the Lorentzian has a lower peak and much stronger wings: it falls as $1/\nu^2$, the Gaussian as $e^{-\nu^2}$. Far from line centre the homogeneous part always dominates. ::: {#tbl-broadening .cell tbl-cap='Order of magnitude of the broadening mechanisms in the lasers of this chapter (FWHM).' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} nu_hene = lz.c0/632.8e-9 rows = [("He–Ne 632.8 nm", "natural, τ ≈ 100 ns (homogeneous)", f"{lz.lifetime_fwhm(100e-9)/1e6:.1f} MHz"), ("He–Ne 632.8 nm", "Doppler, 400 K (inhomogeneous)", f"{lz.doppler_fwhm(nu_hene, 400, 20.18)/1e9:.2f} GHz"), ("CO₂ 10.6 µm", "Doppler, 400 K", f"{lz.doppler_fwhm(lz.c0/10.6e-6, 400, 44)/1e6:.0f} MHz"), ("CO₂ 10.6 µm", "pressure, 1 atm (homogeneous)", "≈ 4 GHz"), ("Nd:YAG 1064 nm", "phonon collisions, 300 K (homogeneous)", "≈ 120 GHz (0.45 nm)"), ("Nd:glass 1054 nm", "site-to-site disorder (inhomogeneous)", "≈ 7 THz (25 nm)"), ("Er³⁺:silica 1530 nm", "Stark splitting + disorder (mixed)", "≈ 4 THz (30 nm)"), ("GaAs laser diode", "intraband scattering ≈ 0.1 ps (homogeneous)", f"{lz.lifetime_fwhm(0.1e-12/2)/1e12:.1f} THz")] pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["laser", "mechanism", "linewidth"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Spectral hole burning (slide 82) A strong beam at $\nu_s$ saturates the atoms it interacts with. In a homogeneous medium every atom sees the beam, so the whole gain curve drops. In an inhomogeneous medium only the atoms whose own (homogeneous) line overlaps $\nu_s$ are saturated: a **hole** appears in the gain curve, of width $\Delta\nu_h\sqrt{1+I/I_\text{sat}}$. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof hb = Inputs.form({ hom: Inputs.range([0.02, 3], {value: 0.15, step: 0.01, label: "homogeneous FWHM / inhomogeneous FWHM"}), I: Inputs.range([0, 50], {value: 5, step: 0.5, label: "saturating intensity I/I_sat"}), nus: Inputs.range([-1.5, 1.5], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "saturating frequency (units of inhomogeneous FWHM)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false hbOut = { const G = 1/(2*Math.sqrt(Math.LN2)), gam = hb.hom/2, Lr = d => gam*gam/(d*d + gam*gam); // L normalised to 1 at centre const N = 401, data = [], cls = d3.range(N).map(i => -2.5 + 5*i/(N - 1)), w = cls.map(c => Math.exp(-(c*c)/(G*G))); let norm = 0; for (let k = 0; k < N; k++) norm += w[k]*Lr(cls[k]); // unsaturated gain at line centre, for normalisation for (let i = 0; i <= 300; i++) { const nu = -2 + 4*i/300; let g0 = 0, g = 0; for (let k = 0; k < N; k++) { const l = w[k]*Lr(nu - cls[k]); g0 += l; g += l/(1 + hb.I*Lr(hb.nus - cls[k])); } data.push({nu, g: g0/norm, who: "unsaturated"}, {nu, g: g/norm, who: "with saturating beam"}); } return {data}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 280, x: {label: "ν − ν₀ (units of the inhomogeneous FWHM)"}, y: {label: "gain (normalised)", grid: true}, color: {legend: true, range: ["#c3c2b7", "#2a78d6"]}, marks: [Plot.line(hbOut.data, {x: "nu", y: "g", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleX([hb.nus], {stroke: "#e34948", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})] }) ``` Make the homogeneous width larger than the inhomogeneous one: the hole widens until the whole curve sinks uniformly. This is the key difference of slide 83. In a **homogeneous** medium the first mode to reach threshold clamps the gain everywhere and the others stay below threshold: single-mode operation (Nd:YAG, in principle). In an **inhomogeneous** medium each mode burns its own hole and several modes lase at once (He–Ne). In a He–Ne laser each mode burns two holes, at $\nu_m$ and $2\nu_0-\nu_m$, because the standing wave interacts with atoms moving in both directions. Spatial hole burning in the standing wave breaks the single-mode rule of homogeneous media in practice. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Lifetime broadening from a Fourier transform.** Sample $E(t)=e^{-t/2\tau}\cos\omega_0t$ for $t\ge0$, take `np.fft.fft` and fit a Lorentzian to $|E(\nu)|^2$. Check that the FWHM is $1/2\pi\tau$. - **Spatial hole burning.** In a standing-wave cavity the intensity has nodes every $\lambda/2n$. Atoms at the nodes are not saturated by the lasing mode and provide gain for a second mode. This is why Nd:YAG lasers are multimode unless they use a ring cavity or a twisted-mode cavity. - **Inhomogeneous broadening in semiconductors?** The gain of a bulk semiconductor is homogeneously broadened by fast intraband scattering (0.1 ps). Quantum-dot lasers, with their size distribution, are strongly inhomogeneous: they lase on many modes and are used for frequency combs. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - Kasap, sec. 4.7–4.8; Siegman, *Lasers*, ch. 3 (line shapes), 12 (saturation) and 16–19 (Gaussian beams and transverse modes). - Saleh and Teich, ch. 3 (Hermite–Gaussian beams) and 15. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Compute the natural linewidth of the ruby R₁ line ($\tau=3$ ms) and compare with its measured 330 GHz width at room temperature. What broadens it? 2. The output of a TEM$_{00}$ laser is clipped by a circular aperture of radius $w$. What fraction of the power passes? What fraction of a TEM$_{11}$ mode? 3. Show that the Voigt FWHM tends to the Lorentzian or Gaussian FWHM in the two limits. 4. In the hole-burning panel, measure the hole width for $I/I_\text{sat}=0,3,8,24$ and check the law $\sqrt{1+I/I_\text{sat}}$.
